chapter_theme: Kaduveli Siddhar's Anandakkalippu is a song of counsel addressed to the mind (மனமே) in the kalippu metre, held together by the refrain 'do no sin, for tomorrow Yama will come in anger and carry you off'. The stanzas alternate plain moral precept (no curses, no anger, no lies, no lust, no begging, do not push away the good) with the Siddhar themes: the body as a bubble and as a potter's pot, the senses as a forest to be burnt, Kasi and the Ganga useless against karma, bhakti above the eight siddhis, the eight and the two discerned within, and the open space of Vedanta reached in a flood of bliss.
structure_note: 1540 is the pallavi, the refrain; 1541 to 1564 are the first twenty-four charanams. The order is loose: 1541 to 1551 are mostly precepts in the negative (லாமோ, ஆதே); 1552 to 1555 turn to the body, the senses and pilgrimage; 1556 to 1563 move toward the goal, the gold without doubt, bhakti, the goddess, the eight and two, the flood of bliss; 1564 returns to prohibitions and runs on into chapter 80.

1540.reading: Do no sin, mind; tomorrow Yama will come in anger, seize you and run off with you.
1540.nuance: The pallavi, repeated after every stanza. The whole song is spoken to the mind as a separate hearer, in the manner of Pattinathar's laments to the heart; the only argument it gives for virtue here is death's nearness, not merit or hell.

1541.reading: Can you lay a curse on anyone? Can fate itself be stopped by us? Can you take up anger? Can you hand over your thought to desire's grip? Four questions, each expecting no.
1541.nuance: The second question is odd among the four: cursing, anger and desire are faults, but 'can we block fate' is a statement of limit. The stanza puts them together as things the mind should not attempt, which makes cursing another futile effort against விதி rather than a sin in itself.

1542.reading: Unspeakable fraud, lies and cheating, if done, bring a ruin that wipes out one's whole kin; good faith kept with great trust earns, every day, the affection of people as one's own.
1542.nuance: The second half is garbled in the text: நல்லபத்த திவிசுவாசம் is taken here as நல்ல பத்தி அதி விசுவாசம் (good faith, great trust), and நம்மையாய் நேசம் perhaps as நன்மையாய் or 'as our own'. The first half is clear: deceit's ruin falls on the family, not only on the doer.

1543.reading: This body is a bubble on water; it will not stay but go, and you should know this illusion. Great love for the earth: devise the means to stay without clinging to it even a little.
1543.nuance: உபாயம் (means, stratagem) asks for a method of non-attachment, not merely a resolve; the song later supplies candidates: bhakti (1558), the goddess's feet (1559), the eight and two (1562).

1544.reading: A mendicant in the garden begged the potter for four-six months, brought back one pot, and dancing and dancing he dropped it and broke it.
1544.nuance: A parable with no key given in the text. Tradition reads the garden as the world, the mendicant as the soul, the potter as the Lord, the pot as the body, and நாலாறு மாதம் as four-six, that is twenty-four months or, with 'and' understood, the months of gestation; the dancing is the pleasure-seeking life that breaks the body. On the plain reading it is only a story of a beggar who smashed what he waited for.

1545.reading: Do not speak slander; not a speck of the wealth you seek will stay with you; the three bound by writ and oath are evil; if you set your desire on Siva, Yama's world is powerless.
1545.nuance: ஏடாணை மூன்றும் பொல்லாதே is unclear; ஏடு and ஆணை may be the written bond and the oath, and 'the three' something the song does not name, perhaps the three desires (மண், பெண், பொன்). பொல்லாதே at the end of two lines must carry two senses, 'is evil' and 'cannot hurt', which supports reading the last clause as Yama's world losing its force over one who desires Siva.

1546.reading: Seek the good way; every day seek the Supreme with longing; join the company of the able; praise and celebrate that generous one in your heart.
1546.nuance: வல்லவர் கூட்டம் is the company of the capable or the realised; the stanza makes company a discipline, as 1564 and 1565 make bad company a danger.

1547.reading: Do not push away the good; of the thirty-two dharmas seek at least one and do not let it drop; take nothing from the wicked; do not let evil, lying tales find a place.
1547.nuance: அறம் நாலெட்டு, four eights, is the traditional list of thirty-two charities (feeding, water-sheds, medicine and the rest). The stanza asks for a minimum, one of thirty-two, which is modest beside the song's yogic claims.

1548.reading: Stand by the rule of the Veda; go the way the good walk, seeking it; speak only what fits the state of things; and the vile, outcaste anger, subdue it and kill it.
1548.nuance: சாத நிலைமையே சொல்லு is unclear; சாது (fitting, gentle) is one reading, so 'speak what is fitting'. The stanza calls anger சண்டாளம், using a caste name as abuse, while 1572 asks the hearer to know all castes as one. The approval of the Veda here is qualified by 1564, which warns against the false Veda; the song keeps the Veda and rejects its false teachers.

1549.reading: Do not ask for anything as alms; do not swell and perish in lust for beautiful women; do not let desire rule you; having climbed the way that Siva desires, do not turn back.
1549.nuance: The refusal of begging is notable in a mendicant tradition, and matches Pattinathar's resolve to beg only of Siva. சிவன் இச்சை கொண்ட அவ்வழி sets Siva's desire against the hearer's: the one இச்சை that may rule is Siva's.

1550.reading: Climb the path of true knowledge; be clear in the pure, open space of Vedanta; revile the way of ignorance; and to those who come near you, tell the way that is bliss.
1550.nuance: வெட்டவெளி, the cut-open space, is the Siddhars' name for the goal as formless expanse; here it is called Vedanta's. The last line turns the hearer into a teacher, which the song's own form, counsel to a mind, enacts.

1551.reading: Do not go past the true guru's word; do not hold back from doing good more and more; do not walk by false arts; do not lead a good intellect down a false road.
1551.nuance: பொய்க்கலை, false arts, probably means fraudulent learning or showmanship rather than the sixty-four arts; the Siddhar catalogues of frauds (Sivavakkiyar's last chapter) give the background.

1552.reading: Nothing comes along with you; taking up this bag of worms and toiling here is the trouble; the hard-sought release is the goal, and no one is clear about the way to seek it.
1552.nuance: புழுக்கூடு, a nest or bag of worms, is a standard Siddhar name for the body. The last line is unusually frank: the song admits that the way to release is not clear to anyone, even as it goes on to give counsel.

1553.reading: A forest surrounded by five; a land that the five reach for these five; seek it beforehand, taking trouble; if you know that root, the house of release comes.
1553.nuance: A coded stanza. Tradition takes the forest as the body, the five who surround it as the senses, the second five as their organs or the five elements, and மூலம் as the root centre at the base of the spine; on this reading the land is the inner place the senses are drawn into. The plain sense is only that one must know the root of the body's business before release.

1554.reading: Within is a fourfold fort; if you take it so that the enemy flees, you can rule the land; the forest called the thieving senses, cut it, set fire and burn it, and you can see the house.
1554.nuance: நால்வகைக் கோட்டை is read by tradition as the four inner faculties (மனம், புத்தி, சித்தம், அகங்காரம்), to be captured; the senses are கள்ளப் புலன், thieves. The verse pairs a siege and a forest-burning, two images of the same inward war; who the fleeing enemy is, the senses or desire, is not said.

1555.reading: Will karma leave you if you go to Kasi? Will bathing in the Ganga give you a good end? Will your deeds die as you speak? Though you praise it, will the manifold difference of being born go away?
1555.nuance: Four rhetorical questions against pilgrimage and holy bathing, the Siddhars' common target. பல பேதம் பிறப்பது, being born in many differences, makes rebirth, not sin, the thing the Ganga cannot wash off.

1556.reading: The show that is falsely celebrated, all of it will go; the time of going comes to everyone; if you bring about on earth a time that is truly pure, what a help that is.
1556.nuance: என்ன அனுகூலம் can be an exclamation (what a benefit) or a question (what benefit is there), and the stanza's point turns on it. கோலம் is outward adornment or display, which places this with 1568 and 1573 on false guises.

1557.reading: The gold that is beyond doubt: if one joins it there is a swelling that knows no lowness, an endless height, a fullness filled everywhere with bliss.
1557.nuance: The Supreme is named only as தங்கம், gold, and the stanza is all nouns of plenitude (பொங்கம், துங்கம், புங்கம்). The alchemical register is deliberate in a Siddhar: the true gold is not the alchemist's but the one that fills everything.

1558.reading: Highest on earth is bhakti; for those who hold to it, release comes to them; the renowned eight siddhis come to anyone by Siva's act, through bhakti.
1558.nuance: The eight siddhis are made a by-product of devotion and of Siva's doing (சிவன் செயலினால்), not of technique. This is the song's ranking: bhakti first, release its fruit, powers an aside.

1559.reading: Scattering the good flower called love, reaching the twin feet of the goddess of supreme bliss, with joy, body and life, seek your uplift here every day, rejoicing.
1559.nuance: The only stanza to name the goddess, பரமானந்த தேவி; the flower offered is love, not a plucked flower, which answers the song's rejection of outward rite. இங்கே, here, places the uplift in this life.

1560.reading: Seeing the uplift that works, knowing the way to it and taking it, doing service without wrath to the Primal Siva, that service will join you to him.
1560.nuance: சீற்றமில்லாமல், without wrath, is an odd condition on service and recalls 1541 and 1548: the song treats anger as the fault that spoils even devotion.

1561.reading: The dance is danced by the soul; only when the soul has left the body does the body wilt; set your gaze on the heavenly state, and every day on earth a celebration will come to you.
1561.nuance: The body is a dancer moved by the soul, which picks up the dancing mendicant of 1544. The promise of daily கொண்டாட்டம் on earth is one Kudhambai's refrain (1599) asks the knower to do without.

1562.reading: Weighing the eight and the two, discerning all the Vedas as one within you, reaching the open space, plunging in the flood of bliss, your joy grows great.
1562.nuance: எட்டும் இரண்டும், the eight and the two, is a Siddhar cipher: by tradition the Tamil letters அ (written like the numeral 8) and உ (like 2), so the syllable ஓம், or more broadly the Lord as அ and the soul as உ. The stanza does not explain it; it only says that discerning it makes the Vedas one within.

1563.reading: This world and what is within it, push them away always without setting any desire on them; scoop up that flood of red honey, and take it in until your thought turns sweet and is sated.
1563.nuance: உள்ளு in the first line is unclear (within, or 'think'); செத்தேன் is read as செந்தேன், red honey, the Siddhars' usual figure for the nectar held to flow within in yoga. தெவிட்ட, to the point of surfeit, is a pointed word: the one thing the song permits the mind to take to excess.

1564.reading: Do not look at the false Veda; do not let the words of those preachers enter your understanding; do not go near the dark-eyed women; do not join in gladness the crowds of those on the wrong road.
1564.nuance: பொய்வேதம் is the false Veda, not the Veda called false: 1548 tells the hearer to stand by Vedic rule. The target is the போதகர், the preachers of it, which keeps the song short of Sivavakkiyar's rejection of the four Vedas themselves.

links.note: The Naladiyar sees the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts, and praises those who resolve to end their wandering; Kaduveli calls the body a bubble on water and asks the mind for a means to stay unattached. The Naladiyar's bubble argues for ending rebirth, Kaduveli's for a method of non-clinging in this life.

Tirumular's potter shapes pots from the tank's clay and notes that a broken pot's shards are kept while a broken body is not; Kaduveli's mendicant begs a pot of the potter and breaks it dancing. Both make the body a potter's vessel, but Tirumular's point is how the dead are discarded, Kaduveli's that the living break the body by their own revelling.

Pattiragiriyar asks to become the Lord's subject before this salted pot breaks and takes a womb again; Kaduveli tells of the pot begged from the potter and broken in dancing. Both poets make the body a pot that will break; Pattiragiriyar adds the return to the womb that Kaduveli leaves out.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will burn the sastras and make the four Vedas false in order to see the one formula; Kaduveli tells the mind to stand by the rule of the Veda. The conflict holds if Kaduveli's வேத விதி means the Vedic injunctions themselves; it softens if 1564's 'false Veda' shows he means only a true core against false teachers, but even then he keeps what Pattiragiriyar burns.

The Kural says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; Kaduveli tells the mind to subdue and kill the vile anger. Both make anger the fault to be destroyed outright rather than measured; Kaduveli adds a caste slur to name it, which the Kural does not.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see with resolve the bare void that grew in the open space and become clear; Kaduveli tells the mind to become clear in the pure open space of Vedanta. The same வெட்டவெளி and the same verb of clearing (தேறு, தெளிவு), but Kaduveli names it Vedanta's, which Pattiragiriyar elsewhere leaves behind.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they have done; Kaduveli says nothing comes along at all, and that bearing the body is itself the trouble. The Naladiyar's exception for deeds is what Kaduveli's own pallavi relies on, since Yama comes for sin, so his flat 'nothing' is rhetorical, not a denial of karma.

Pattiragiriyar asks when, burning off the five senses in which the ego hides, he will gain bliss; Kaduveli tells the mind to cut the forest of thieving senses, set fire and burn it to see the house. Both burn the senses; Kaduveli adds the siege of the fourfold inner fort as the step before.

The Kural makes understanding an inner fortress that enemies cannot destroy; Kaduveli has a fourfold fort within that must be captured from the enemy before one can rule the land. The Kural's fort is a possession that protects; Kaduveli's is held by the enemy and must be stormed, so the same image runs in opposite directions.

Pattinathar asks his heart what ash and bathing are worth when it has not learned the way to be born differently, lying in the river without knowing the ford; Kaduveli asks whether Kasi and the Ganga remove karma or the manifold difference of being born. Both tie the futility of bathing to rebirth, not only to sin.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart, and that the deceitful who do not bathe in them wander over hollow and height; Kaduveli asks whether going to Kasi or bathing in the Ganga ends karma. Both deny the outer river's power; Tirumular supplies the inner bathing that Kaduveli only implies.

Tirumular says the eight great siddhis are not hard for him because the Lord gave grace and cut off his birth; Kaduveli says the eight siddhis succeed for anyone by Siva's act through bhakti. Both make the powers a consequence of grace rather than a goal of technique, and both set release or the cutting of birth above them.

Sivavakkiyar says that if one regards within oneself the god who became the linga when eight and two joined, one crosses the sea of birth; Kaduveli says that weighing the eight and the two and discerning the Vedas as one within, one reaches the open space and the flood of bliss. Both place the eight-and-two cipher inside the body and make it the key to the goal.

Tirumular says to know by gathering the eight and the two and set Nandi within knowledge; Kaduveli says to weigh the eight and the two and find the Vedas one within. Both treat the cipher as something gathered inwardly; Tirumular adds the five who danced becoming kin, Kaduveli the open space and the flood of bliss.

source_issues: 1542: நல்லபத்த திவிசு வாசம் and நம்மையாய் நேசம் are garbled; the second half of the stanza is read conjecturally.
1545: ஏடாணை மூன்றும் பொல்லாதே is obscure and may be corrupt.
1563: உள்ளு (line 1) and செத்தேன் (line 3, probably செந்தேன்) look miscopied.
